translations.text: It is very right for us to praise with words the Guardian of the skies, the glorious King of hosts, and to love him in our hearts! He is the abundance of all powers, the head of all high creations, the Lord almighty.
There was never any beginning for him, no origin came into being, nor will an end ever come now for the eternal Lord, but he will always be mighty over the heavenly thrones.
In high majesty, true and abundantly bountiful, he held the expanses of the sky, which were set wide and broad through the power of God for the children of glory, the guardians of spirits.
The troops of angels had radiance and joy, and had their Creator, a bright bliss. Great was their glory!
The glorious thanes praised their Prince, spoke praise gladly, and glorified their Lord of life; they were greatly blessed in the excellences of the Lord.

They knew no sins, nor how to commit crimes, but they lived in peace, eternally with their Lord. They began to raise up nothing else in the heavens except right and truth, until a guardian of angels strayed into error through pride.

They would no longer follow their own good, but they turned away from the kinship-love of God. They made a great boast that, with the might of their host, they could share with the Lord the glorious dwelling, vast and heaven-bright.

Pain befell them there, envy and pride, and the mind of that angel who first began to carry out that evil counsel, to weave it and stir it up, when he said in words, thirsting for malice, that he would possess a home and a high throne in the northern part of the kingdom of heaven.

Then God became angry and wrathful with that host which he had earlier honoured with beauty and glory. He shaped for the traitors a home of exile as reward for their deed, the laments of hell, hard afflictions.

Our Lord commanded that house of torment to await the exiles, deep and without joy, the guardians of spirits [?], when he knew it ready, enclosed in perpetual night, filled with torment, filled throughout with fire and sudden cold, smoke and red flame.
Then he commanded terror of punishment to grow throughout that counselless house. They had grimly gathered a hostile band against God; a grim reward came to them for that!
They said, fierce-minded, that they would possess the kingdom, and could do so easily.
That hope deceived them, once the Ruler, the high King of the heavens, raised his hands, highest against that host.
The thoughtless ones, wicked against the Creator, could not wield their strength, but the glorious one cut off their courage and bowed down their arrogance.

Then he became enraged; he stripped the sinful foes of victory and power, glory and dignity, and deprived his enemy of joy, peace and all gladness and bright honour, and he avenged his anger fiercely on his adversaries by his own powers, with a mighty overthrow [?].
He had a stern mind; grimly angered, he seized them in wrath with hostile hands and, furious at heart, broke them in his grip. The noble one cut his adversaries off from their glorious dwellings.
Then our Creator thrust out and cut off from the heavens the proud race of angels, the faithless host.
The Ruler sent the hateful host on a long journey, those sad spirits. Their boast was crushed, their vow shattered, and their power brought low, their beauty defiled.

Afterwards they lingered in darkness in exile; they had no cause to laugh aloud, but they dwelt weary in the torments of hell and knew woe, pain and sorrow; they suffered torment, covered in darkness, a harsh retribution for having begun to strive against God.
Then there was truly peace in heaven as before, fair customs of peace. The Lord was dear to all, the prince to his thanes. The glories of the hosts who possessed joy with the Lord increased.

Those who dwell in the sky, the homeland of glory, were then in harmony. Strife had ended, and so had terror and warlike hatred among the angels, since the warmongers had left heaven, deprived of light.

Behind them the seats in God's kingdom stood wide, rich in glorious abundance, flourishing with gifts, bright and prosperous, without inhabitants, after the accursed spirits had gone, abject, to the place of exile under the prison of harm.

Then our Prince considered in his mind how he might establish again the glorious creation, the ancestral seats, the heaven-bright halls, with a better host, since the boastful foes had abandoned them, high in the heavens.

Therefore holy God, with mighty powers, set to work beneath the heavens; he willed that earth and the sky above and the wide water should be established for him as the creation of the world, in place of the hostile ones whom he had cast out of his protection as rebels.
Nothing had yet come into being here except hidden shadow. This wide ground stood deep and dim, estranged from the Lord, empty and useless.

The steadfast King looked on it with his eyes and beheld the place, without joys. He saw dark gloom brooding in endless night, black under the heavens, murky and waste, until this created world came into being through the word of the King of glory.
Here the eternal Lord, protector of all creatures, the Lord almighty, first created heaven and earth. He raised up the sky and established this spacious land with strong powers.

The earth was then not yet green with grass. The ocean covered the dark waves far and wide in black, endless night. Then the glory-bright spirit of heaven's guardian was borne over the sea with great power.

The Creator of angels, the giver of life, commanded light to come forth over the spacious ground. The high King's command was quickly fulfilled. Holy light was there over the wasteland, as the Maker had ordered.
Then the Ruler of victories separated light from darkness over the water-flood, shadow from radiance. Then the giver of life made names for both.

Through the Lord's word, light, a beautifully bright creation, was first named day. That fruitful time, the first day, pleased the Lord well at the beginning. He saw the dark shadow, black, recede across the wide ground.
When that time had passed, hastening away over the frame of the middle-earth, the Creator, our Maker, sent the first evening after the bright radiance.

Dark mist pressed and ran on its track, to which the Prince himself gave the name night. Our Saviour separated them. Ever since then they have carried out and done the Lord's will, eternally over the earth.
Then came the second day, light after darkness. Then the guardian of life commanded a delightful heavenly structure to come into being in the middle of the sea-flood.
Our Ruler divided the waters and made the firmament of the skies. The mighty one, the Lord almighty, raised it up from the earth through his own word.
The flood was divided by holy powers under the high firmament, water from the waters that still remain under the stronghold, the roof of the peoples.
Then the glorious third morning came over the earth, eager on its journey. The wide lands and the ways were not yet of use to the Creator, but the earth stood firmly covered by flood.
Through his word the Lord of angels commanded the waters to be gathered together in an appointed place, the waters that now keep their course under the heavens.
Then the sea quickly stood under the heavens, wide and all together, as the holy one had ordered, when water was separated from land.
Then the guardian of life, the shepherd of hosts, saw dry land, widely revealed, when the King of glory named it earth.

He set for the waves, the spacious flood, their proper course, and fettered [?]. Then it did not seem fitting to the guardian of the heavens that Adam, the keeper and guardian of paradise, the new creation, should be alone any longer.
Therefore the high King, the Lord almighty, provided a helper for him. The light-source of life brought forth a woman and gave that support to the beloved man.
He separated that material from Adam's body and skilfully drew a rib out of his side.

Adam was fast at rest and slept softly. He felt no pain and no share of hardship, and no blood came from a wound there. The Prince of angels drew the growing bone out of his body and left the man unwounded, and from it God made a noble woman.
He put life into her, an eternal soul. They were like angels. Then Eve, Adam's bride, was furnished with a spirit.
Both of them were born into the world in youth, beautifully bright, by the Creator's powers. They did not know how to do or suffer evil, but love of the Lord burned in the hearts of both.
Then the glad-hearted King, the Ordainer of all creatures, blessed the first two of humankind, father and mother, woman and man. Then he spoke these words:
"Now be fruitful and increase, and fill the ever-green earth with offspring, with your kind, sons and daughters. The salt water and all the creation of the world shall remain in your power."

Enjoy the days of plenty, and the burden of the sea, and the birds of heaven. To you two are given into your power the holy livestock and the wild beasts, and the living things that tread the land, the kinds endowed with life, and those that the flood brings forth throughout the whale-road. All things obey you."
Then our Creator surveyed the beauty of his works and the abundance of his fruits, the new creations.
Paradise stood good and spiritual, filled with gifts and lasting benefits. Water ran fairly through that pleasant land, a welling spring.
The clouds did not yet carry rains over the wide ground, dark with wind, yet the earth stood adorned with fruits. Four noble streams ran forth from the new paradise.
Then, by the Lord's powers, all were divided out of one when he created this earth, with water of bright beauty, and he sent them out into the world.
People, the dwellers on earth, call one of these the Pishon. With its bright streams it encircles that part of the land, Havilah, broadly from outside.
In that homeland, as books tell us, the children of the nations of men find gold and gems, the best of them, near and far.
Then the second river surrounds from outside the land and dwelling-place of the people of Ethiopia, a spacious kingdom. Its name is Gihon.
The third is the Tigris, a river full in flood, which flows around the people of Assyria.
Likewise there is the fourth, which men now widely call the Euphrates among many peoples.
"But enjoy all the rest. Leave that one tree alone and guard yourselves against its fruit. You two shall have no lack of delights."

Then they eagerly bowed their heads toward the King of heaven and gave thanks for everything, for his skills and his teachings. He let them live in that land. Then the holy Lord, the stern-minded King, turned back to the heavens.
His handiwork stood together on the sand. They knew nothing of sorrow to lament, as long as they carried out God's will. They were dear to God while they were willing to keep his holy word.

The Ruler of all, the holy Lord, had by the might of his hand established ten orders of the race of angels. He fully trusted that they would follow him in service and do his will, because he, the holy Lord, had given them understanding and shaped them with his hands.
He had placed them so blessedly. He had made one of them so strong and so mighty in his mind's thought, and he let him rule so much,
…highest next to himself in the kingdom of heaven. He had made him so bright, and so lovely was the form that came to him in heaven from the Lord of hosts, that he was like the bright stars.

He ought to have praised the Lord. He ought to have held his joys in heaven dear, and ought to have thanked his Lord for the reward that he had granted him in that light. Then the Lord would have let him rule it for a long time.
But he turned it to something worse for himself, and began to raise up strife against the highest Ruler of heaven, who sits on the holy throne.

He was dear to our Lord. It could not be hidden from the Lord that his angel began to grow overproud. He raised himself up against his master and turned to hateful speech and boastful words against him.
He would not serve God. He said that his body was bright and beautiful, white and bright of hue. He could not find it in his heart to serve God, his Prince, as a follower.
It seemed to him that he had more strength and power of companions than the holy God could have.
The angel of pride spoke many words. He thought about how, by his own strength alone, he might make himself a stronger throne, higher in the heavens.
He said that his mind urged him to begin building in the west and north and to set up structures. He said he doubted that he would remain God's subordinate.
"Why should I toil?" he said. "I have no need at all to have a master. I can work as many wonders with my own hands.
"I have great power to prepare a more godly throne, a higher one in heaven. Why should I serve for his favour, or bow to him in such subjection? I can be a god as well as he.
Strong companions stand by me, hard-minded warriors, who will not fail me in the struggle.
These brave warriors have chosen me as their lord. With such men one can plan a course of action and take up with such comrades.
They are my eager friends, loyal in their thoughts. I can be their lord and rule in this kingdom.
So it does not seem right to me that I should need to flatter God at all for any good thing. I will no longer be his follower."
When the Almighty had heard it all, how his angel had begun to raise great pride against his master and had spoken haughty words foolishly against his Lord,
…he had to pay for that deed and take his share of the pain of that strife, and he had to have his punishment, the greatest of all torments.
So does every man who begins to strive wickedly against his Ruler, against the glorious Lord. Then the Mighty One, the highest Ruler of heaven, became enraged and threw him down from the high throne.

he had earned hatred from his master and lost his favour. The Good One grew angry with him in his heart. Therefore he had to go down to the depths of the hard torment of hell, because he had fought against heaven's Ruler.
Then he cut him off from his favour and threw him into hell, into the deep pits, where he became a devil, the fiend together with all his companions.
Then the angels fell from heaven above, for as long as three nights and days, from heaven into hell, and the Lord changed them all into devils.
Because they would not honour his deed and word, almighty God therefore set them, without victory, in a worse light down beneath the earth, in the black hell.

There, in the evening, each and every one of the fiends has fire renewed for an immeasurably long time; then at dawn comes the east wind, frost fiercely cold. Always fire or piercing cold [?]: they had to endure some hard torment.

It was made for them as a punishment (their world was overturned): for the first time he filled hell with the adversaries. From then on the angels who had kept God's favour before held the heights of the kingdom of heaven.
The other fiends, who had earlier waged so much strife against their Ruler, lay in the fire.
They suffer torment, hot surging fire in the midst of hell, burning and broad flames, and likewise the bitter smoke, fumes and darkness, because they neglected the service of God.
Their wantonness deceived them, the angel's pride; they would not honour the word of the All-Ruler; they had great torment.

Then, because of their folly and their pride, they had fallen through fire to the bottom, into hot hell. They had come to another land, one that was without light and full of flame, a great terror of fire.
The fiends perceived that they had received in exchange countless torments through their great presumption and through the might of God, and most of all through their arrogance.

Then the proud king spoke, he who had once been the most beautiful of angels, the brightest in heaven, beloved of his Master and dear to the Lord, until they turned to folly, so that God himself, mighty in mind, became angry with him for his arrogance.

He threw him into that destruction, down into that bed of death, and afterwards gave him a name: the Highest said that from then on he should be called Satan. He commanded him to keep watch over the abyss of the black hell, and not to strive against God.
Satan spoke; sorrowing he said, he who from then on was to hold hell and keep watch over the abyss:
He had once been God's angel, bright in heaven, until his mind and, most of all, his pride led him astray, so that he would not honour the word of the Lord of hosts.
His thoughts welled up within him around his heart, and outside him was hot and cruel punishment. Then he spoke these words:

"This narrow place is very unlike the other home that we knew before, high in the kingdom of heaven, which my Lord granted me, though because of the All-Ruler we were not allowed to possess it or to extend [?] our realm.
Yet he has not done right in casting us down to the bottom of the fire, of the hot hell, deprived of the kingdom of heaven. He has marked it out to be settled with mankind.
That is the greatest of sorrows to me: that Adam, who was made of earth, shall hold my mighty throne and live in joy, while we suffer this torment, this harm in this hell.
Alas! If I had the power of my hands and could get out for one hour, be out for one winter's hour, then I with this host— But iron bonds lie about me, the rope of chain rides me.
I am stripped of my kingdom. The fetters of hell have seized me so hard and hold me fast. Here is a great fire, above and below. I never saw a more hateful landscape.
The flame does not die down, hot over hell. The clasp of rings, the cruelly hard rope, has kept me from moving and taken away my going; my feet are bound, my hands fettered.
The ways out through these doors of hell are blocked, so that I cannot by any means get free of these limb-bonds. Great bars of hard iron, forged hot, lie about me.

For God has fettered me by the neck, and so I know that he knew my mind. The Lord of hosts also knew that things would go badly between Adam and me over the heavenly kingdom if I had the use of my hands.
But now we suffer torments in hell (they are darkness and heat), grim and bottomless. God himself has swept us into these dark mists.
Although he cannot charge us with any sin, any harm we did him in that land, he has still cut us off from the light and cast us into the greatest of all torments.
We cannot take vengeance for this, or repay him with any harm because he has cut us off from the light.
He has now marked out a middle-earth, where he has made man after his likeness. With him he means to fill the kingdom of heaven again with pure souls.
So we must think hard about how we may avenge our grievance on Adam, if we ever can, and on his offspring as well, and turn them away from his will there, if we can devise it in any way.
I no longer hope for that light which he thinks to enjoy for a long time, that bliss with the strength of his angels. We can never achieve it, that we should weaken the mind of mighty God.

Let us now turn it away from the children of men, that kingdom of heaven, now that we may not have it; let us bring it about that they give up his favour, so that they overturn what he commanded with his word.
then he will grow angry with them in his mind and cast them out of his favour. Then they will have to come to this hell and these grim depths.
Then we can have them as our servants, the children of men, in these fast fetters. Now begin to think about the expedition!
If in former days I ever gave princely treasures to any thane while we sat happy in that good kingdom and held our thrones, then he could never repay my gifts at a more welcome time,
if any of my thanes would still agree to it, so that he could come up and out of here through these prison bars, and had the power in him to fly with a feather-coat,
than by flying up through the sky to where Adam and Eve stand, created, in the earthly kingdom, surrounded by riches, while we are cast down here into these deep valleys.

Now they are far more precious to the Lord, and they may possess the wealth that we should have had in the kingdom of heaven, the realm that was ours by right. That gift has been allotted to the race of men.
It is so painful to me in my mind, and it grieves me in my heart, that they are to possess the kingdom of heaven forever.
If any of you can bring it about in any way that they abandon God's word and his teaching, they will soon become more hateful to him.
If they break his command, then he will become enraged with them. After that their prosperity will be taken away, and punishment will be prepared for them, some harsh and grievous fate.
All of you, think about how you might deceive them! Then I can rest easy in these chains, if they lose that kingdom.
Whoever accomplishes this will have a reward ready for him afterwards forever, from whatever benefits we can win in here, in this fire, from now on.
I will let him sit beside me, whoever comes into this hot hell to tell me that they have [?] the heavenly King's teaching unworthily in words and deeds." Then God's adversary began to equip himself.
eager in his gear (he had a treacherous mind), he set a helmet of concealment on his head and bound it very tightly, fastening it with clasps. He knew many speeches of crooked [?] words.
He swung up from there and went through the doors of hell (he had a strong mind). Hostile in mind, he flew through the air and split the fire in two with a fiend's power.
He wanted to deceive the Lord's followers, the humans, in secret with wicked deeds, and to mislead and lead them astray so that they became hateful to God.

He then travelled by a fiend's power until he found Adam on earth, God's handiwork, ready and wisely made, and with him his wife, the fairest woman, as they knew how to do much good [?], whom the Lord of mankind had himself marked out as his servants.
And beside them stood two trees, laden on the outside with fruit and covered in produce, just as the ruling God, the high King of heaven, had set them there with his hands,
so that there the children of men, every one of them, could choose between good and evil, prosperity and woe. The fruit of the two trees was not alike!

The one was so pleasant, beautiful and bright, gentle and praiseworthy: that was the tree of life. Whoever bit into that fruit could live on afterwards into eternity and remain in the world, so that old age would not harm him after that,

nor grievous sickness. Instead he could always live straight away in delights and keep his life and the favour of the King of heaven here in the world, and have, as a pledge, the honours appointed to him in high heaven when he departed from here.

The other tree was entirely black, dim and dark: that was the tree of death, which bore much bitterness. Every man who ate of it would have to know both evil and good, the difference between them in this world.
Whoever tasted what grew on that tree would have to live ever afterwards in punishment, with sweat and with sorrows.
Old age was to take from him his deeds of courage, his joys and his lordship, and death was to be allotted to him.
He would enjoy his life for only a little while, and then go to the blackest of lands, in fire.
He would have to serve fiends, where the greatest of all dangers lies for people for a long time. The hateful one knew that well, the devil's secret messenger, who had fought against the Lord.

Then by the devil's power he took on the body of a serpent and wound himself around the tree of death. He took some of the fruit there and turned back from there to where he knew the handiwork of the King of heaven was.
Then the hateful one, full of lies, began to question him with his first words: "Adam, do you long for anything up there with God?
I have travelled here from far away on his errand, and it was not long ago that I sat beside him.

Then he ordered me to go on this journey. He ordered that you eat this fruit, and said that your strength and skill and your understanding would become greater, and your body much brighter, and your form more beautiful. He said that you would never need any wealth in the world.
"Now you have done his will and won the favour of heaven's King. You have served your Lord in a way that pleases him, and you have made yourself dear to the Lord.
I heard him praise your deeds and words in his light and speak about your life.
So you must carry out whatever his messengers bring here to this land. The green dwelling-places in the world are broad, and God, the Ruler of all, sits above in the highest kingdom of the heavens.
The Lord of men does not wish to take on the hardship of making this journey himself, so he sends his servant to speak with you.
Now he has commanded me to teach you skills by my message. Be eager to carry out his commands. Take this fruit in your hand, bite it and taste it.
Your heart will grow spacious and your form will become fairer. God the Ruler, your Lord, has sent you this help from the kingdom of heaven."

Adam, the man God made himself, spoke where he stood on the earth: "I heard the Lord of victory, mighty God, speak with a strong voice. He commanded me to stand here and keep his commandments, and he gave me this bride,

a woman of radiant beauty. He commanded me to beware that I should not be led astray [?] by the tree of death and be badly deceived. He said that whoever brought anything hateful into his heart would have to dwell in black hell.

"I do not know whether you come with lies out of some secret purpose, or whether you are the Lord's messenger from heaven. I cannot understand anything of your commands, your words or your ways, your journey or your sayings.
I know what he himself, our Saviour, commanded me when I last saw him. He commanded me to honour his word, keep it well and follow his teaching.
You are not like any of his angels that I have seen before, and you have not shown me any token that my lord sent me in faith and grace.
Therefore I cannot obey you, and you may go on your way. I keep firm faith in almighty God above, who made me with his arms, here with his own hands.
From his high kingdom he can give me every good thing, even without sending his servant."

He turned away in anger to where he saw the woman, Eve, standing on the earth, beautifully formed. He told her that the greatest of harms would afterwards come upon all their descendants in the world:

"I know that God the Ruler will become angry with you two when I return from this journey over the long road and report this message to him myself: that you do not carry out properly any errand he sends here from the east on this journey.
Now he will have to come himself to get your answer, because his messenger cannot deliver his errand. So I know that he, mighty in mind, will be angry with you.
But if you, willing woman, will listen to my words, then you can think of a generous remedy for this.
Consider in your heart that you can save both of you from punishment, as I guide you.

Eat of this fruit! Then your eyes will become so bright that from then on you will be able to see far and wide over the whole world, and even the throne of your Lord himself, and you will have his favour from now on.
Afterwards you will be able to guide Adam, if you have his goodwill and he trusts your words.

Tell him truthfully what example you have in your own heart, because you have carried out God's command and teaching. Then he will give up the hateful quarrel and the wicked answer in his heart, since the two of us will be speaking to him with one purpose.
Urge him eagerly to follow your teaching, so that you two will not become hateful to God, your Ruler.
If you accomplish this undertaking, best of women, I will hide from your Lord how much harm Adam spoke to me and how many base words he used.
He accuses me of being untrue and says that I am eager to do harm, a servant of the hostile ones, not God's angel at all.
"But I know all the orders of angels and the high vaults of the heavens very well. I served God eagerly for a long time with a loyal mind, my Lord, the Lord himself. I am not like a devil."

So he led her on with lies, and with cunning he enticed the woman into that wrong, until the serpent's counsel began to boil within her (the Creator had given her a weaker mind), so that she began to let her mind follow his teachings.
So, against the Lord's word, she took from the hateful one the painful fruit of the tree of death. No worse deed was ever ordained for humankind!
It is a great wonder that eternal God, the Prince, would ever allow so many a servant to be led astray by the lies that came as teaching.
Then she ate of the fruit and broke the word and will of the Almighty. Then she could see far and wide, through the gift of the hateful one who had deceived her with lies and secretly beguiled her,

a gift that came to her through his deeds, so that heaven and earth seemed brighter to her, and all this world more beautiful, and God's work great and mighty, though she did not see it through human thought.

but the enemy worked hard to deceive the soul to whom he had earlier lent that sight, so that she could look so far across the heavenly kingdom. Then the accursed one spoke out of enmity (he did not advise them for their good at all):
"You can now see for yourself, so that I do not need to tell you, good Eve, that your beauty and form have changed since you trusted my words and carried out my teaching.
Now a light shines before you, gladdening, facing you, which I brought from God, bright from heaven; now you can touch it.
Tell Adam what vision and what powers you have through my coming. If he still carries out my teachings humbly, then I will give him enough of that light with which I have so well adorned you.
I will not blame him for those insulting words, though he does not deserve to be let off, so many hateful things he said to me."
So her offspring must live after her: when they do wrong, they must work love, make amends for their lord's insult, and have his favour from then on.

Then the loveliest of women went to Adam, the fairest of wives who ever came into the world, for she was the handiwork of the King of heaven, though she had then been secretly ruined, led astray with lies,

so that through the hostile one's counsel they would become hateful to God, and through the devil's cunning would lose glory and their Lord's favour, and be deprived of the kingdom of heaven for a long while.
Full woe is the man who does not guard himself while he has the power to!
She carried some of the unblessed apple in her hands, and some lay at her heart: the fruit of the tree of death, which the Lord of lords had forbidden her before.
And the Prince of glory had spoken that word, saying that people, his servants, need not suffer that great death, but the holy Lord gave the kingdom of heaven, wide-reaching wealth, to every people,
if they would leave alone that one fruit which the hateful tree bore on its boughs, filled with bitterness. That was the tree of death, which the Lord forbade them.

Then the one who was hateful to God deceived her with lies, out of hatred for heaven's King. He deceived the mind of Eve, the weak thought of the woman, so that she began to trust his words and to follow his teaching,

and she came to believe that he had brought those commands from God, which he told her so carefully in words. He showed her a sign and promised her his good faith and his loyal intent. Then she spoke to her lord:

"Adam, my lord, this fruit is so sweet and gladdening in the breast, and this messenger is shining, God's good angel. I see from his clothing that he is a messenger of our Lord, heaven's King. It is better for us two to win his favour than his hostility.
If you said anything harmful to him today, he will still forgive it, if we two are willing to serve him.
What good is such hateful quarrelling with your lord's messenger? We need his favour; he can carry our message to the Almighty, the King of heaven.
From here I can see where he who made this world sits himself (that is, to the south and east), surrounded by riches.

I see his angels circling around him in feathered robes, the greatest of all peoples, the most joyful of hosts. Who could give me such understanding if God, the Ruler of heaven, had not sent it directly?

I can hear far and wide, and see so widely over all the world, over this broad creation; I can hear the joy of heaven in the heavens. It has grown light in my mind, outside and inside, since I bit into the fruit.
"Now I have it here in my hand, good lord; I give it to you gladly. I believe that it came from God, brought at his command, as this messenger told me with true words."
It is not like anything else on earth, except as this messenger says: that it came directly from God."
She spoke to him again and again and urged him all day toward the dark deed, that they should break their Lord's will.
The hostile messenger stood there, laid desires upon him and enticed him with cunning, pressed after him boldly. The fiend who had made that perilous expedition over a long road was very near.

[?] he intended, in that great murder, to cast the people down, to mislead them and lead them astray, so that they would give up God's loan, the gift of the Almighty, the rule of the heavenly kingdom.
Lo, the hell-fiend knew well that they would have to receive God's anger and the torment of hell, and of necessity suffer that harsh affliction, once they had broken God's command,
when with lying words he misled the fair lady, the most beautiful of women, into that bad counsel, so that she spoke according to his will; God's handiwork was a help to him in leading them astray.
Then the fairest of women spoke to Adam again and again, until the man's mind began to turn, so that he trusted the promise that the woman told him in words.

Yet she did it with a loyal heart. She did not know that so many harms and terrible afflictions would follow for mankind because she took it into her mind to listen to the teachings of the hateful messenger.

but she thought that she was winning the favour of the King of heaven with the words by which she showed the man such a sign and promised him good faith, until Adam's mind turned within his breast and his heart began to turn toward her will.
From the woman he received hell and death, though it was not called that; it had to bear the name of fruit.
Yet it was the sleep of death and the devil's enticement, hell and death and the ruin of men, the murder of mankind, that they took as food, that evil fruit.
As soon as it came inside him and touched his heart, the bitter-minded messenger laughed and capered about, and gave thanks for both of them to his lord:
"Now I have surely earned your favour for myself and carried out your will for many a day to come. The humans are led astray, Adam and Eve.
The Ruler's anger is fixed on them, now that they have abandoned his command and his teaching. Therefore they can no longer hold the heavenly kingdom, but must go to hell on that dark journey.
So you need not carry sorrow for it in your breast where you lie bound, nor grieve in your mind that men dwell here in the high heaven,
while we two now suffer harms and torments and the land of darkness, and through your great pride many gave up the lofty buildings in the heavenly kingdom, the goodly dwellings.
God became angry with us two because in the heavenly kingdom we would not bow our heads to him, the holy Lord, as his followers; it did not suit us to serve him as his vassals.

Therefore the Ruler became angry in mind with us two and harsh in spirit, and drove us into hell. He filled that fire with the greatest of hosts, and with his own hands he set up the heavenly thrones again in the heavenly kingdom and gave that kingdom to the race of men.

Your mind may be glad in your breast, for here both things have been done: the children of men, the people, must give up the heavenly kingdom and turn into that hot flame to you, and also harm has been done to God and grief caused to his heart.
Whatever torment we two suffer here, it is now all repaid on Adam with the Lord's hatred and with the ruin of men, on humankind with the agony of death.
Therefore my mind is healed, and my spirit is at ease around my heart. All our harms are avenged, the injury that we two have long suffered.
Now I will go back nearer to the flame; I will seek Satan there. He is held captive in that dark hell with the fastening of chains."
The most bitter messenger turned back downward; he had to seek the broad flames, the slopes of hell, where his lord lay forever bound.

The two of them, Adam and Eve, grieved, and they often exchanged words of lament between them. They feared God, their lord's hatred; they greatly dreaded the enmity of the King of heaven. They themselves understood that his word had been overturned.

The woman mourned and lamented, sorrowful in mind (she had forsaken God's favour and his teaching), when she saw that light glide away elsewhere, the light that he who had counselled them to that injury had shown her as a sign of faithlessness,
so that they would have to suffer the hostility of hell, countless humiliations; therefore sorrows of mind burned in their breasts.

At times the married pair fell to prayer together, and they hailed the good Lord of victory and called on God, the Ruler of heaven, and asked him that they might take his punishment and eagerly carry it out in full, since they had broken God's command.

They saw that their bodies were bare. In that land they did not yet have settled dwellings, nor did they know any of the sorrow of labour; they could have lived well in that land if they had been willing to carry out God's teaching continually.
Then they spoke many sorrowful words together, the married pair, the two of them.
Adam spoke and said to Eve: "Lo, Eve, you have marked out an evil fate for the two of us.
Do you see now the dark hell, greedy and ravenous? Now you can hear it raging from here.

The kingdom of heaven is not like that fire. But this is the best of lands, which we two might have kept by our Lord's grace if you had not listened to the one who counselled us to this harm, so that we broke the word of the Ruler, the King of heaven.
Now we two, sorrowful, may grieve for this fate. For he himself commanded us to guard ourselves against punishment, the greatest of harms.
Now hunger and thirst tear at me bitterly in my breast, though before we were both free of these cares at all times.
How shall we two live now, or survive in this land, if the wind comes here from west or east, south or north?
Dark cloud rises up, a shower of hail comes pressing down from heaven, and frost comes along with it, terribly cold.
At times the heavens shine hot, this bright sun blazes, and we two stand here naked, with no clothing to protect us.
We have nothing in front of us as shelter from the storms, and nothing set aside for food. Instead the mighty God, the Ruler, is angry with us. What will become of us now?
Now I may regret that I asked the God of heaven, the good Ruler, to make you here for me from my own limbs, now that you have led me astray into my Lord's hatred.
So now I may regret for ever and ever that I ever saw you with my eyes."
Then Eve spoke in turn, the fairest of women, the most beautiful of wives. She was God's handiwork, though she had then been deceived by the devil's craft:
"You may blame me for it with your words, my dear Adam. Yet it cannot grieve you any worse in your mind than it grieves me in my heart."

Then Adam answered her: "If I knew the Ruler's will, and what punishment I must take from him, you would never see anything quicker than I would be, even if the God of heaven commanded me to wade into the sea from here right now, [?]
…to travel on the flood, were it ever so terribly deep, the sea-stream ever so great, that my mind would never doubt it [?], but I would go to the very bottom, if I could carry out God's will.
I have no need in the world of any service, now that I have lost my Lord's favour, so that I cannot have it.
But we two cannot stay here naked together like this to any purpose. Let us go into this forest, into the shelter of this wood."

The two of them turned and went away mourning into the green forest. They sat apart and waited for their fate from the King of heaven himself, since they could no longer have what almighty God had given them before.
Then they covered their bodies with leaves and clothed themselves with the forest, since they had no garments.

…but they fell to prayer, both of them together, every morning. They prayed the Mighty One, God almighty, not to forget them, and prayed that the good Ruler would guide them in how they should live from then on in that light.

Then the Lord almighty, the glorious Prince, came walking into Paradise after midday, for his own purpose. Our Saviour, the merciful Father, wished to see what his children were doing. He knew that those to whom he had once given beauty had fallen into sin.
Then they went off, sad at heart, under the shade of the trees, robbed of their glory. They hid themselves in darkness when they heard the holy word of the Lord, and they were afraid.
Then at once the Prince of the heavens, the Guardian, began to question the creatures of the world. The mighty Prince ordered his son to come to him quickly.
Then he himself answered him; the wretched man, lacking clothing, spoke: "I cover myself here, without garments, my Lord of life; I cover myself with leaves.
"Guilty, my [?] is painful to me, dangerous in my mind. I dare not go forth now into your presence. I am all, all naked."
Then God answered him at once: "Tell me this, my son: why are you seeking the shade in shame? You never received disgrace from me before, but joy in all things.

Why do you know woe and cover your shame, see sorrow, and cover your body with leaves yourself? Why do you say, wretched and sad at heart in your anxiety for your life, that you need clothing, unless you have tasted an apple from the forest-tree that I forbade you with my words?"
Then Adam answered him again: "My bride, the lovely woman, gave the fruit into my hand, my lord and master, and I accepted it, to your injury.
Now I carry a clear sign of it on myself. I know sorrow all the more."
Then almighty God asked Eve about it: "What have you done, daughter, with the plentiful benefits, the new creations of paradise, the growing gifts,
"... when you greedily grabbed at the tree, took fruit from the tree's branches, and ate that harmful thing to my injury, and gave Adam the fruit that was firmly forbidden to you both by my words?"
Then the lovely maiden, the woman, ashamed, answered him: "The serpent deceived me and eagerly urged me to wrongdoing and to sinful greed, the hostile serpent, with fair words,
until I shamefully carried out the fiend's plan and brought about enmity. Then I robbed the tree in the grove, which was not right, and ate the fruit."
Then our Saviour, the almighty Lord, decreed wide wanderings for the serpent, the hostile reptile, and spoke these words:
"You shall forever crawl, weary, on your breast and belly over the broad earth, and go without feet as long as life, the spirit within you, remains.

You shall eat dust for the days of your life. Because you so hatefully stirred up strife, the woman shall loathe you and hate you under the heavens, and she shall tread on your head, hostile one, with her feet.

You shall lie in wait for her heels in new strife. Hostility shall be shared between the offspring of you two forever, as long as the world stands under the clouds. Now you know and understand, hateful destroyer of people, how you must live."
Then God spoke angrily to Eve: "Turn away from joy!

You shall be in a man's power, harshly constrained by fear of your husband. Wretched, you shall suffer for the folly of your deeds and await death. Through weeping and lamentation, and through great pain, you shall bring sons and daughters into the world."
The eternal Lord, the Source of the light of life, also announced a hateful message to Adam:
"You must seek another homeland, a more joyless dwelling, and go into exile, naked and needy, deprived of the joys of Paradise. The separation of body and soul is ordained for you.
Lo, you hatefully stirred up strife. Therefore you shall toil and obtain your food on earth yourself, with a sweating face, and eat your bread
while you live here, until the cruel disease that you yourself swallowed earlier in the apple grips your heart hard. Therefore you shall die."
Lo, now we hear where our grievous harms and worldly miseries cruelly began.
Then the Guardian of glory, our Creator, clothed them with garments. The Lord commanded them to cover their shame with the first clothing. He ordered them to leave paradise for a narrower life.

Behind them, at the Lord's command, a holy angel locked with a fiery sword the hopeful home of comforts and joys. No man full of malice and stained with sin may go there, for the guardian, who keeps that glorious life, precious in its blessings, for the Lord, has might and strength.

Yet the Almighty, the Father from the beginning, did not wish to deprive Adam and Eve of all his favours, even though they had fallen away from him. Instead, for their comfort, he still let the roof adorned with holy stars remain, and he gave them the spacious riches of the earth.
He commanded sea and earth to bring forth fruits for the married couple, for every family of the offspring-bearing creatures, for use in the world.
Then, after their sin, they settled in a sorrowful land, a homeland and native region poorer in every good thing than their first home, from which they had been driven out after their deed.
Then, at God's command, they began to beget children, as the Creator had commanded them.
Two noble firstborn children were born to Adam and Eve first: Cain and Abel. Books tell us how those first workers, the dear brothers, gained riches, wealth and food.
One of them, the firstborn, worked the earth with vigour; the other kept livestock to help his father, until a great number of days had passed.
Then they both brought offerings to the Lord. The Prince of angels, the King of all creatures, looked with his eyes on Abel's offering; he would not look at Cain's sacrifice.
That was a grief to the man, heavy at his heart. A surge of passion rose up in the man's breast: livid hatred, anger out of envy.
Then with his hands he did a wicked deed: Cain slew his kinsman, his brother Abel, and shed his blood. The earth swallowed that slaughter-blood, the man's gore.
After the deadly blow, woe was raised up, an offspring of sorrows. From that branch hateful, cruel fruits afterwards grew, more and more strongly the longer it went on.

The branches of strife spread far among the nations of men. The shoots of harm struck the children of men hard and painfully (they still do), and from them the broad blades of every evil began to sprout.

We may tell that tale, that cruel and deadly fate, with weeping, and not without cause. But the noble woman did us great harm through the first sin that men, the dwellers on earth, ever committed against the Creator, after Adam was given a spirit from God's mouth.
Then the Lord of glory asked Cain where on earth Abel was.
Then the wicked worker of death answered him at once: "I do not know Abel's coming or going, my kinsman's journey, nor was I my brother's keeper."

Then the prince of angels, the spirit rich in power, answered him: "Listen! With your angry hands you have laid a faithful man, your brother, on a bed of slaughter, and his blood calls and cries out to me.
For that killing you will suffer punishment and go into exile, cursed forever.
The earth will not give you fair fruits for worldly use, for it swallowed holy blood of slaughter from your hands. Therefore the green earth will deny you its comforts and its splendour."
You shall wander in sorrow, without honour, away from your homeland, because you became Abel's slayer. Therefore you must travel far-wandering paths as an outcast, hateful to your kinsmen."
Then Cain answered him at once: "I need not expect any mercy in the kingdom of the world, for, high King of the heavens, I have lost your favour, your love and your friendship.
So I must travel far and wide, expecting misery, until someone meets me, guilty of crime as I am, and far or near reminds me of the feud, of my brother's murder.
I shed his blood, his gore, on the earth. Today you cut me off from all good fortune and drive me from my homeland.
Some hostile man will become my killer. Lord, I must go away from your sight, cursed."
Then the Lord of victories himself answered him: "You need not fear the terror of death, of violent death, yet, though you must go, guilty, far from your kinsmen.
If any man takes your life with his hands, sevenfold vengeance will come upon him for that sin, punishment for the deed."

The Ruler, the glorious Measurer, the Lord, set a token on him, a sign of protection, so that none of his enemies would dare to attack him with violence in battle, from far or near. Then he commanded the guilty man to go away from his mother and kinsmen, from his own kindred.

Then Cain went, sad at heart, out of God's sight, a friendless exile. He chose himself a dwelling in the eastern lands, a homestead far from his father's home, where a noble woman, a lady of high birth, bore him children.

The first, Cain's firstborn, was called Enoch. Afterwards Cain began to build a stronghold, a city, with his kinsmen. Of all the walled fortresses under the heavens that princes, sword-bearers, ordered to be built, that was the first.
There, in that city, his descendants first arose, children born of his bride.
The eldest was called Jared, son of Enos. After that the family of Cain arose, those who increased the generations of that race.
After Irad, Mehujael kept the inheritance, following in his father's footsteps until he passed away.
Afterwards Methuselah shared out the princes' treasure to his kinsmen, child after child, to his brothers, until, old and full of years, he had to meet his parting from life and give up his life.
After his father's day Lamech received the household goods and the treasures of the home. Two wives, ladies in that land, bore him children: Adah and Zillah.
One of these was named Jabal, son of Lamech. Through his wise thought, he was the first of those who dwell here to waken the sound of the harp with his hands, a melodious music.

In that same family, at that same time, there was also a kinsman named Tubal-cain. Through the wealth of his wisdom he was a skilled smith, and through the thought of his mind he was the first of men,
this son of Lamech, to begin the work of the plough on earth. After that the children of the peoples, the city-dwellers, learned to make wide use of brass and iron.
Then Lamech himself told a shameful tale to his two wives, his beloved bedfellows, Adah and Zillah:
"I have murdered one of my kinsmen. I have defiled my hands in the killing of Cain. With my hands I struck down the father of Enos, the slayer of Abel, and gave a man's slaughter-blood to the earth.
I know well that after this killing will come the sevenfold vengeance of the true King, great after the crime. My fall and death will be repaid more severely, with grim terror, when I go forth."
Then another son was raised for Adam in that land in place of Abel, a righteous son, whose name was Seth.

He was blessed, and he grew up as a noble comfort to his parents, his father and mother, Adam and Eve. He was the recompense for Abel in the kingdom of the world. Then the first of mankind spoke these words:

"The Ruler of victories himself, the Lord of life, has given me an eternal son in place of the beloved one whom Cain killed. With this offspring our Prince has driven care and sorrow from my mind. Thanks be to Him for this!"
When Adam, the courageous man, began again to beget for himself another child by his bride, as an heir to his homeland, he had [lived] a hundred and thirty [years] of this life, winters in the world.

Writings tell us that here on earth Adam afterwards increased his family with women and men for eight hundred [years]. In all he had lived nine hundred and [?] winters when he had to give up this world through the parting of the soul.

After him Seth ruled the people, the son after his parents. He held the ancestral seat and took a wife. He was a hundred and five winters old when he first began to increase the people of his family with sons and daughters.
The eldest son of Seth was called Enos. He was the first of all the children of men to call upon God by name since Adam, endowed with spirit, stepped on the green grass.

Seth was blessed. Afterward, for eight hundred and seven winters here, he begot sons and daughters. In all he had [lived] nine hundred and twelve [years] when the time came that he had to make his departure from life.
When he departed from the world, Enos held the inheritance after him, once the earth had swallowed the body of Seth, the seed-bearer.
He was dear to God and lived here ninety winters before he begot children by his wife through marriage. Then Cainan was born to him, his first son in the homeland.

Afterward, for eight hundred and fifteen [years] in the peace of the Lord, the wise-minded man begot young offspring, sons and daughters. The old sage died when he had [lived] nine hundred and five [years].
After Enos, Cainan was then the chief ruler of that kindred, its guardian and leader. He had lived exactly seventy winters before a son was born to him.
Then a son was brought up in the homeland, Cainan's offspring, who was called Mahalalel.

Afterward, for eight hundred and forty more [years], the son of Enos increased the number of princes with new lives. In all he had nine hundred and ten winters when he gave up the world, when the count of his days under the expanse of the heavens was fulfilled.
After him Mahalalel held the land and inheritance for many half-years.

The chieftain had sixty-five winters when he began to beget children by his wife. His bride, the woman, brought a son into the world of men. As I have heard, that son was called Jared, a young man among his kin.
Mahalalel lived long afterward and enjoyed delights here, the joys of men and the treasures of the world.
He had eight hundred and ninety-five winters when he passed away, and he left the land and the rule of the people to his son. For a long time afterward Jared distributed gold to men.
That nobleman was noble, a pious man, and the chieftain was dear to his kinsmen.
He lived in the kingdom of the world for a hundred and five winters, and sixty more, before the time came when his wife brought a son into the world. The son was called Enoch, a noble firstborn.
Here the father still went on increasing the number of his descendants for eight hundred [years]. In all he had [lived] sixty-five,
and nine hundred as well by the reckoning of nights, the friend old in winters, when he gave up this world. Jared then left the land and the rule of the people to the wise one, his beloved man.
Afterward Enoch took up the rule, the leader of the people, prosperous in peace. He did not let glory and lordship decline at all while he was guardian of the chief kinsmen.
He enjoyed glorious days and begot children for three hundred winters. The Lord, the Ruler of the heavens, was gracious to him.
From here that man went in his body to seek grace, the company of the Lord. He did not die the death of middle-earth at all, as men here do, young and old,

when God takes from them their possessions and sustenance, the treasures of the earth, and their life with them. Instead he departed alive with the King of angels from this passing life, to travel in the garments his spirit had received before his mother brought him into the world of men.
He left the people to his eldest son, his firstborn. He had sixty-five winters, and three hundred as well, when he left the world.

Afterward, for a time, Methuselah held the inheritance of his kinsmen. Of all these men, he enjoyed the joys of the world in the body the longest. Before his day of death he begot a great many sons and daughters.
When the old man had to depart from men, he had nine hundred winters, and seventy more besides. His son Lamech held the people's land after him, and ruled the world for a long time afterward.
He had a hundred and two winters when the time came that the nobleman began to beget noble offspring, son and daughter.

After that he lived ninety-five and also five hundred years: the lord, the chief of the host, enjoyed many winters under the heavens. He ruled the people well and fathered children. Sons were born to him, both sons and daughters.
He named the eldest Noah, who ruled the land among men after Lamech passed away.
The wise leader of nobles was five hundred years old when he first began to father children, as the books say.

The eldest son of Noah was called Shem, the second Ham, the third Japheth. Peoples multiplied widely under the heavens, and the number of the tribes of men grew throughout the world through sons and daughters.
The race of Seth, the beloved leader of the people, was still very dear to the Lord in love and blessed with glory, until the sons of God began to look for brides among the race of Cain,
a cursed people. There, against the Creator's will, the sons of men chose wives for themselves, women of the guilty ones, bright and fair.
Then the Ruler of the heavens, angry with mankind, spoke these words: "The descendants of Cain have not gone free from my mind; that race has angered me sorely.

Now the sons of Seth renew my anger, and they take the women of my enemies as wives for themselves. There the beauty of the women, the faces of the women, and the eternal enemy have fiercely invaded the people of men, who were at peace before."

After that, for a hundred and twenty winters by count, the doomed peoples busied themselves with wickedness in the world, until the Lord chose to inflict punishment on the oath-breakers and strike dead the giants, who were guilty in their deeds, unloved by God, great evildoers, hateful to the Measurer.
Then the Ruler of victories himself saw how much human wickedness there was on the earth, and that the people were bold in sin and full of malice.
He resolved to punish that foulness on the generations of men, and to seize mankind grimly and sorely with his harsh might.

He bitterly regretted that he had raised up the founder of the peoples, the first of nobles, when he created Adam. He said that because of men's sins he would destroy everything on earth, destroying every body that the breath of life held in its embrace.
The Lord intended to kill all of it at the coming time, which was then drawing near for the children of men.
Noah, the son of Lamech, was good, dear to the Saviour, greatly blessed, steadfast in judgment and righteous. The Lord knew that this noble man's courage and the thoughts of his heart were sound;

therefore the Prince, the Protector of all creatures, holy in his speech, told him what he intended to do to men in his enmity. He saw the earth full of wrongdoing, the broad dwelling-places laden with sins and defiled with filth.
Then the Ruler, our Saviour, spoke and said to Noah: "I will destroy the people with a flood, along with every kind of living creature that air and water bring forth and feed, cattle and birds.
You will have protection with your sons when the black water, the dark streams of death, swallow up the hosts, the guilty wrongdoers.
"Begin to build yourself a ship, a great sea-house. In it you must make room for many to rest, with a proper place for each of earth's offspring according to its own kind.
Build decks inside the ship.
Build that vessel fifty ells wide, thirty high and three hundred long, and build it to withstand the waves, joining it firmly together.
Into that wooden fortress the seed of every kind of living creature must be brought, the offspring of the earth's breed; for that reason the ark must be the larger."
Noah did as the Saviour had commanded him. He obeyed the holy King of heaven and quickly began to build that house, the great sea-chest.
He told his kinsmen that a dreadful thing was coming upon the peoples, a cruel punishment. They paid no attention to it!
Then, after many years, the faithful Creator saw the greatest of ocean-houses towering up, ready, sealed inside and out against the flood with earth's lime of the best kind: Noah's vessel.
That is a special kind; the harder the rough water and the dark sea-currents beat against it, the harder it always becomes.

Then our Saviour said to Noah: "Dearest of men, I give you my pledge of this: that you will set out on your way, carrying the offspring of the living creatures you must bring, over the deep water for a great number of days in the ship's hold.
"As I command you, lead your offspring under the ark's deck: your three chief sons, and the four of you with your wives.
And take into that sea-hall seven, counted by number, of every kind that lives as food for men, and two of each of the others.
Also bring provisions from all the fruits of the earth under the deck for the people who are to survive the sea-flood with you."
Feed the offspring of living creatures generously until, after the sea-voyage, I choose to make room again under the heavens for food for the survivors.
Go now with your household into that dwelling, with the company of souls. I know you to be good and steadfast of mind; you are worthy of protection and of mercy, together with your children.
Now, after seven nights, I will let deadly rain fall from above onto the face of the wide earth.

For forty days I will bring hostility on men, and with a host of waves I will destroy all possessions and their owners that are outside the boards of the ark when the black storm-cloud begins to rise."
Then Noah went, as the Saviour commanded him, to lead his sons under the deck of the ark, the men onto the ship, and their wives with them;
and everything that the Lord Almighty wished to have for breeding went under the roof to the one who would feed them, as the Almighty Lord of hosts had commanded him by his word.
Behind him the Guardian of the heavenly kingdom, the Ruler of victories, closed the door of the sea-house with his own hands, and our Saviour blessed the inside of the ark with his own powers.
Noah, son of Lamech, was six hundred winters old when he went on board with his children, wise with the young ones, at God's command, with his dear company.
The Lord sent rain from the heavens, and he also let springs pour abundantly into the world from every vein, and let dark ocean-streams roar. The seas rose up over the shore-walls.

Strong and fierce was he who ruled the waters. Because of their wicked enmity he covered and roofed over the children of the earth with the dark wave, over the homeland of men. He ravaged their dwellings; the Ruler avenged on men the injury done to his heart.

The sea gripped the doomed people hard for forty days and as many nights. The punishment was fierce, deadly and grim to men. The waves of the King of glory drove the life of the wicked out of their bodies.

The flood, rough beneath the heavens, covered all the high mountains across the wide earth. It lifted the ark up from the earth onto the water, and with it the noble ones whom the Lord himself, our Creator, had blessed when he shut up that ship.

After that the best of dwellings rode far and wide under the clouds over the ring of the sea and travelled with its cargo. The terrors of the water could not strike violently at the seafarers with sudden danger, for holy God carried them and saved them.
The drowning flood stood fifteen ells deep, by a man's measure, over the hills. That is a famous event!
In the end there was nothing to separate them, except that heaven was raised up into the high air, when the ocean-host had killed all the offspring of the earth.
except that the Lord of the heavens held up the ark's timbers, when holy God, the eternal one, the stern-hearted King, let the flood climb up in its streams and lifted it up, humble [?].
Then God, the Ruler of victories, the source of the light of life, remembered the seafarer, the son of Lamech, and all the offspring he had shut in against the water in the ship's bosom.

Then the Lord of hosts guided the warrior by his word over the wide land. The surging flood began to lessen again. The water ebbed, dark beneath the sky. The true Ruler had turned the ocean-stream back for the children, back to its bright course, and had stilled the rain.

The foaming ship travelled a hundred and fifty nights under the heavens after the flood lifted up the nail-boarded vessel, the best of ships, until the counted number of days of that fierce time had passed.
Then the greatest of sea-houses, Noah's ark, came to rest high with its cargo on the mountains that are called Armenia.

There the holy one, the son of Lamech, waited a long time for the true promises to be fulfilled, waiting for when the Guardian of life, the Lord Almighty, would give him rest from his perilous journeys. He had endured them far and wide when the dark waves carried him on the sea across the wide earth.

The sea was going down. The men, the seafarers, and their wives as well, longed for the time when they might step out of their confinement over the nail-boarded side onto the shore and lead their possessions out of that narrow place.
Then the ship's captain tested whether the sinking sea-flood still lay beneath the clouds.
Then, many days after the high slopes had received the treasure, and also the noble ones of the earth's offspring, the son of Lamech let a black raven fly out of the house over the deep flood.

Noah reckoned that if the raven found no land on that journey, it would have to seek him out again over the wide water on the ship. But that hope deceived him, for the bird perched gleefully on a floating corpse; the dark-feathered one would not seek him.
Then after seven nights he let a grey dove fly out of the ark over the high water, after the black raven, to test whether the deep, foaming sea had yet given up any part of the green earth.

She searched far and wide for what she wanted and flew a long way. But she found no rest: because of the flood she could not set her feet on land or step onto a tree's leaves because of the streams. Instead the steep slopes were covered with water.
In the evening the wild bird went back to look for the ark over the dark waves. Weary and hungry, she sank down into the hands of the holy man.
Then after a week the wild dove was sent out of the chamber again. She flew far and wide until, rejoicing in the open space, she found a fair resting place and set her feet on a tree.
She rejoiced, glad at heart, that in her great weariness she could sit on the bright branches of the tree.
She shook her feathers and went flying back with her gift. The flier brought a single twig of an olive tree to his hands, with green leaves.
Then the lord of the seafarers quickly understood that comfort had come, a remedy for their hard journeys. After a third week the blessed man again sent out a single wild dove.

She did not come flying back to the ship. Instead she reached land and the green groves. Once she no longer needed to, the glad bird never again wished to show herself under the dark deck in the fortress of planks.

Then our Saviour, the Guardian of the kingdom of heaven, spoke to Noah with holy voice: "A homeland is opened to you again, a pleasant place on land, rest from voyages on the water, fair upon the earth.

Go out in peace from the ark, and from the high dwelling lead your household onto the bosom of the earth, and all the offspring that I saved on the ship in the distress of the waves, while the water had covered the third homeland with its might."
He did so and obeyed the Lord. With great joy he climbed over the ship's side, as the voice commanded him, and led out of the wave-ship the remnant left from the wrath.

Then Noah, firm in counsel, began to set up a sacrifice to the Savior on the altar. Wise in making the offering, he quickly took a share of all the possessions that the Lord had given him for his prosperity. Then the bright-minded man offered a sacrifice to God himself, the King of angels.

Indeed, when our Savior blessed Noah and his sons together, he made it known that Noah had given that offering in thanks. He had also earned it earlier by good deeds in his youth, so that almighty God, glorious in judgment and majesty, granted him the favor of all blessings.
Then the Lord, the Prince of glory, spoke further to Noah: "Now be fruitful and multiply. Enjoy glory and peace with joy. Fill the earth and increase all things.
Into your power are given the homeland, the burden of the sea, the birds of heaven, the wild beasts, the ever-green earth and abundant cattle.
Never shall you dishonorably eat your table meals with blood, defiled with sin and with life-blood.
Anyone who takes another's life with the point of a spear first deprives himself of the blessings of the soul.

He will have no reason to rejoice in his heart at that reward. I will demand a man's life from the slayer far more strongly, and from the killer of his brother, from whoever succeeds in shedding blood, in slaughtering a man with weapons, in murder by his own hands. Man was first created in the likeness of God.
Everyone who is willing to keep holy ways has the likeness of the Creator and of the angels.
Grow and flourish. Enjoy what you desire and the blessings on earth. Fill the regions of the earth with your noble offspring, with descendants and children.
I give you my pledge that I will never again bring a host of the sea, water over the wide land, upon the earth."
You may often and frequently see a sign of this in the clouds, when I show my rainbow, that I keep this covenant with men as long as the world stands."

Then the wise son of Lamech had come out of the vessel after the flood with his three sons. He was the keeper of the inheritance, faithful to the Creator, the survivor of the waters. With them were their four wives, who were named Percoba, Olla, Olliva and Ollivani.
The sons of Noah were brave-minded men. They were named Shem and Ham, and the third was Japheth. From these men nations grew, and all this world was filled with the children of men.

Then Noah began anew to establish a home with his kinsmen and to till food for them from the earth. He toiled and worked, planted a vineyard, sowed many seeds, and eagerly sought what the green earth brought him: bright, beautiful fruits, splendid gifts.

Then it happened that the blessed man became drunk with wine in his dwelling. Weary from feasting, he fell asleep, and he himself pushed the clothing off his body. That was not fitting: he then lay there with his limbs naked.
He hardly understood that such a wretched thing had happened to him in his house, since in the holy man's dwelling the dizziness in his head had gripped the heart in his breast.

Deep in sleep his mind was so constrained that, overcome in his senses, he could not cover himself with clothing by his own hands and hide his shame. That covering has been the rule for men and women ever since the thane of glory locked the homeland of life behind our father and mother with a fiery sword.
Then Ham, Noah's son, was the first to go in to where his father lay, robbed of his senses.
There he would not show any kindness or respect to his own father, nor even hide the shame from his kinsmen. Instead, laughing, he told his brothers how the man was lying in the house.
Then they quickly went in with their faces covered, carefully holding cloaks over themselves, so that they could help the man they loved. Both were good, Shem and Japheth.
Then Lamech's son woke from sleep and at once understood that Ham had not wanted to show him, his noble and good father, any loyalty or faithfulness when he needed respect.

That was painful in mind to the holy man. He then began to curse his own son with words, and said that Ham must be lowly under the heavens, a servant of his kinsmen on earth. That sentence afterwards harmed him and his descendants terribly.
Afterwards Noah and his sons, free men after the flood, enjoyed the broad realm for three hundred and fifty winters of this life before he passed away.
After that his sons shared out his wealth and had children. They had splendid riches.
Then the offspring of Japheth was raised, a joyful household of close kinsmen, sons and daughters.
He himself was good. He always kept his kingdom, the joys of his homeland and prosperity among his children, until the treasure in his breast, his spirit eager to leave, had to go to God's judgment.
Then Japheth's son, grieving, shared out his father's household possessions among his friends, his loved ones and his kinsmen. The descendants of that family filled no small part of the earth.
Sons were likewise born to Ham, heirs in the homeland. The eldest were named Cush and Canaan, very noble lives, Ham's firstborn.
By birth Cush was the chief. Following his father, he gave out what his brothers desired: worldly goods and treasures of the house, after Ham had left his body when death struck him.
This leader of young men gave judgments to his tribe until the count of his days had run out. Then the warrior, the father of Nimrod, gave up his earthly wealth and went in search of another life.
Then Cush's firstborn son ruled from the ancestral seat. He was a widely famous man, and the scriptures tell us that in those days he had the greatest might and strength of all mankind.

He was the founder of the mighty kingdom of Babylon, the first of its princes. He raised up the glory of the homeland, enlarged it and built it up. At that time all the people who lived on earth still shared one language.
Many tribes of men likewise came from Ham's line. A great number of descendants were born from that widespread people.
Then many sons and daughters, freeborn children, were born to Shem and raised in the world before the leader of the people, old in years, chose his deathbed.
In that tribe there were good men. One of them was named Eber, the son of Shem. Countless peoples came from that man, whom nobles and all people on earth now call Hebrews.

Then they set out from the east, bringing their possessions, their livestock and their goods. The people were of one mind. Brave warriors looked for more spacious land until they arrived in great bands, a people on the move, at a place where they, the descendants of nobles, firmly settled a home.

Then the leaders of the people settled Shinar, broad and wide. For those beloved people in the days of old, green plains and fair land brought lasting prosperity at that time, with a growing abundance of everything they desired.

Then many a man there, a like-minded noble, asked his kinsman and the others that, for their own glory, before the multitude had to scatter again across the face of the earth as tribes of people searching for land, they should build a city and raise a tower up to the stars of heaven as a sign.
after they sought out the plain of Shinar, as the very mighty leaders of the people, the eldest, often and frequently dwelt there pleasantly;

[?] …by counsels the men turned to work and to wrongdoing, until in their pride and folly they showed their skill: they built a city and raised a ladder up to the heavens, and with their strength they put up a stone wall beyond the measure of men. They were eager for glory, those men, with their hands.
Then holy God came to look at the work of the generations of men, the fortified city of men, and also the tower which the children of Adam had begun to raise up to the heavens,
And the stern-hearted King punished that folly when, fierce of mood, he made the speech of the earth-dwellers unlike, so that their speech did not succeed for them.
When they met in bands at the tower, strong in might and in great numbers, for the business of the work, none of the tribes of men there knew what another said.

They could not build the stone wall any higher, but wretchedly broke apart in bands, divided by their speech. Each kin group had become foreign to the others, after the Creator, through the abundance of his might, scattered the speech of men.
Then the sons of nobles went apart along four ways, divided, in search of land. Behind them both the strong stone tower and the steep city stood together, half-built, in Shinar.
Then the kin of Shem grew and flourished under the clouds, until a man was born in that line, among the number of royal children, a thoughtful man, mindful of virtues.

Sons were born to the nobleman, two noble children brought up in Babylon. Those chieftains, bold-minded men, were called Abraham and Haran. The Lord of angels was friend and lord to both of those men.
Then a son was brought up to Haran, beloved in life, whose name was Lot.

Those young men, Abraham and Lot, prospered before the Lord without reproach, as their nobility in the kingdom of the world had come from their forefathers. For this reason the children of noble nations now honour them far and wide with glory.
When the appointed time had come, Abraham brought a lady home as his wife, to where he had his dwelling, fair and noble. The woman was called Sarah, as books tell us.
Then for many winters they shared the world and their treasure together, and kept peace for a great number of years.
Yet it was still not granted to Abraham that the beautiful lady, Sarah, should bring into the world an heir for him, sons and daughters for Abraham.
Then Abraham's father set out with his family, journeying with provisions across the people of the Chaldeans. Wise, with his kinsmen, he wanted to seek the land of Canaan.
His kinsmen, chosen by the Lord, Abraham and Lot, journeyed with him from that homeland.
Then the noble sons of princes, men with their wives, took a dwelling place in Haran. In those dwellings Abraham's father, a faithful man, gave up his life;
he had two hundred and five winters, counted by number, when he departed, old in years, to see the Lord's decree.

Then the Holy One, the Guardian of the kingdom of heaven, the eternal Lord, spoke to Abraham: "Go now, journey forth and lead your company and your possessions with your family. Leave Haran, your father's homeland.
Go as I command you, dearest of men, and obey my teachings well, and seek the land that I will show you, all green, the broad earth. You shall live blessed under my protection.
If any dweller on earth greets you with woe, I will set my curse on him, and fierce anger, long-lasting enmity. I will give grace, the fruit of their desires, to those who honour you.
Through you all dwellers on earth, the children of the peoples, shall receive peace and friendship, my joy and blessing in the kingdom of the world."
"The number of your kin shall flourish greatly under heaven, in sons and daughters, until the earth becomes [full of] your offspring, and many a nation is filled with your descendants."

Then Abraham departed, leading his possessions out of the borders of Egypt. He was good in noble virtues, very rich in gold and silver, and blessed. As the Guardian of victories, our Ruler, commanded him through his word, he led his cattle from Haran. They sought the land of Canaan and the dwelling place of the people.

Then the one dear to God came into that homeland, leading the women, his beloved bedfellow and his nephew's wife, as he wished. He was seventy-five winters old when he had to set out and leave Haran and his kinsmen.
