Then Abraham went journeying, mindful of the teaching of the Father almighty, to view the land far and wide throughout the nations at the Lord's command, until the courageous man, successful in his journey, came to Shechem, to the race of the Canaanites.

Then the King of angels himself appeared to Abraham, the glorious one of hosts, and the Lord said: "This is the land, all green, bright and rich with fruits, that I will give into the power of your offspring, a spacious kingdom."
Then the man built an altar to God and offered a sacrifice to the Ruler of life, the Source of light, the Protector of souls.

Then Abraham went on from the east to look with his eyes on the choicest of lands. (He remembered the grace of heaven's Guardian's promise, when the King of victories himself had revealed the truth to him through holy word.) He went until the lordly men came with their company to where the rich dwelling place called Bethlehem is.

The man, glad at heart, and his brother's son, devout men, travelled on from the east with their possessions through famous lands and slopes steep as walls. They chose dwellings for themselves where the plains seemed beautiful to them.

Then Abraham built an altar a second time. There, good in his virtues, he called on God with clear words and offered a sacrifice to his Lord of life at that place of fire. (The Measurer did not repay him meagerly for this through His hand.)

There the leader then lived in his dwellings for some time and enjoyed what he desired, the man with his wife, until a terrible calamity came pressing on the people of Canaan who lived in that land: a harsh famine, deadly to men.
Then wise-minded Abraham, chosen by the Lord, went into Egypt to seek a livelihood. The faithful man fled from hardship, for that affliction was too severe.
Abraham spoke. He saw the white gabled halls of the Egyptians and their high cities shining brightly. Then the lord, the wise-minded man, began to instruct his bride with words:

"Once many proud Egyptians are able to look on your beauty with their eyes, the warriors of the nobles will suppose, woman fair as an elf, that you are my bright bedfellow, whom one of those men will want to take for himself.
I may fear that some hostile man will rob me of my life with the edge of a weapon, out of desire for you.
Say, Sarah, that you are my sister, my kinswoman by blood, when foreign men ask you what the bond of love is between the two of us, strangers come from far away.
Firmly hide the true account from them. In this way you will save my life, if the Lord, our Ruler, the one Almighty, grants me protection in this worldly kingdom, a longer life, as he did before.
He shaped this journey for us, so that in Egypt we should seek kindness and benefits, and look for gain for ourselves."
Then the courageous man came journeying into Egypt, Abraham with his possessions, where the people were strangers to him, unknown as friends.
Many proud men, exulting in their wealth, spoke about the woman's beauty. To many of the king's thanes the noble woman seemed splendid in beauty.

They made it known to their lord of the people that few women were fairer [?] before the prince, but they praised Sarah far more, her winsome beauty, with words, until he commanded the lovely woman to be led to his own hall.

The giver of treasure, the protector of nobles, ordered that Abraham be raised up with riches. Yet the Lord, the Master, became hostile and angry toward Pharaoh because of his desire for the woman. The joy of young warriors paid for that grievously and harshly, along with his household.

Yet the lord of men understood why the Ruler punished him with painful scourges. The chief of Egypt, oppressed by terrors, summoned Abraham to him and gave back his bride, returning the wife to his keeping. He told him to choose friends elsewhere, other nobles, another company.
Then the king of the people commanded his thanes, his servants, to bring him back honorably and entirely unharmed out of that territory, so that he would be in peace.

Then Abraham led his possessions out of the borderland of the Egyptians. The courageous men escorted the woman, the bride, and the treasure, so that they led their cattle to Bethlehem, into a familiar dwelling place, with their blessed earthly wealth, a second time, the wife as they wished, and their worldly treasure.
Then they began to build and raise their settlement, to set up a hall and renew their dwellings.
The men set up an altar on the plain near the one that Abraham had earlier raised to his Ruler when he came from the west.

There the blessed man once again honoured the name of the eternal Lord with a new voice; the good-minded man offered a sacrifice to the Lord of angels and thanked the Source of the light of life greatly for his favours and mercies.
Abraham and Lot lived in those dwellings and had plenty of all they wanted.

They enjoyed prosperity until they could no longer share in that wealth together in the land and both keep their possessions there. Instead the honorable men had to seek a homeland elsewhere, with more room.

Often there was injury between the companies of the faithful men, hard and harmful strife. Then holy Abraham, mindful of honor, began to speak kindly to Lot: "I am your father's brother by kinship, and you are my nephew.
Strife must not grow between us two, nor quarrel flourish. May God not will that!
But we two are kinsmen. We shall have nothing else in common except what is wholly good, long-lasting love.
Now, Lot, consider that proud men live around our borders, peoples strong in glory with thanes and companions, the people of the Canaanites and the Perizzites, brave warriors.

Their rights over the land will not give us more room. Therefore we two must lead our people away, move from this place, and seek more spacious lands to settle. I am giving counsel for us both, son of Haran, and I speak the truth.
I leave the choice to you yourself, dear one. Consider for yourself and think in your mind which way you wish to turn, to go with the bargain, now that I have offered you the choice."
Then Lot went to view the land by the Jordan, the green earth.

It was watered by streams and covered with crops, bright with flowing waters, and like God's paradise, until the saving God, because of men's sins, gave Sodom and Gomorrah over to the surging fire, the black flame.

Then the son of Haran chose for himself a dwelling and a home in the city of Sodom; he led away all his possessions, rings from Bethlehem and household treasures, wealth, twisted gold. Afterward he lived by the Jordan for many years.
There the dwelling-places were fair, but the men were wicked, hateful to the Lord.
The people of Sodom were bold in sins and perverse in deeds; they brought about their own eternal ruin.
Lot would never adopt the customs of that people, but he shunned the ways of that tribe, their deceit and crime, though he had to live in that land,
and [he] conducted himself well, virtuous and patient among that people, just as if, mindful of [God's] teachings, he did not know what those peoples did.

Abraham went on living in the homelands of the Canaanites. The King of angels, the Lord of mankind, held him in his protection, with the fruits of his desires and with worldly wealth, with love and with favours;

therefore the generations of men, the children of the earth, speak his praise far and wide under the skies. He obeyed the Lord gladly in his homeland while he enjoyed that land, holy and wise in mind;

never in any matter will a man among living beings be left without shelter, fearful and afraid before the Lord, if he will always seek to please Him afterwards, through abundance of mindfulness, in mind and in deeds, in word and in understanding, with wise thought, until his life's end.
Then I heard that the lord of the Elamites, the bold leader of the people, Chedorlaomer, summoned an army; Amraphel of Shinar went with him from the wide world in support.
Then the four kings of nations set out from there with a great force, going south to attack Sodom and Gomorrah.

Then the homeland of the men by the Jordan was overrun far and wide by war-bands, the land by enemies. Many a frightened, pale-cheeked woman had to go trembling into a stranger's embrace; the defenders of brides and rings fell, sick with wounds.
Then five kings of peoples came against them from the south with warlike force and troops; they wished to defend the city of Sodom against the hostile ones.

For twelve winters before this they had been forced to pay tribute to the northern men and to give taxes, until the people would no longer strengthen the prince of the Elamites with the people's treasures, but revolted from him.
Then they marched together (the spears were loud), the angry slaughter-hosts. The dark bird sang beneath the spear-shafts, dewy-feathered, in hope of carrion.
Warriors hastened in mighty troops, strong in spirit, until the armies of the peoples had come together far and wide from south and north, covered with helmets.
There was hard play, an exchange of deadly spears, a great war-clamour, a loud sound of battle. Warriors drew ring-marked swords, strong of edge, from their sheaths with their hands.
There it was easy for a warrior to find the trade of battle, for any who before had not had his fill of strife.
The northmen were a bane to the southern peoples; the men of Sodom and Gomorrah, the givers of gold, were bereft at the clash of shields of their dear ones, their comrades in arms.
They left the dwelling-place to save their lives by flight, their men slain; in their track fell the sons of nobles, cut down by blades, their dear companions.
The leader of the Elamites won the victory in war and held the field of slaughter. Those left alive by the weapons went to seek a stronghold.
The enemies plundered the gold; with their army they ravaged the treasure-cities of men, Sodom and Gomorrah; at that time the famous cities paid the price.
The women departed, maidens and widows, robbed of their friends, from their place of shelter. The enemies led away, along with the possessions, Abraham's kinsman out of the city of Sodom.

We can tell the truth further, what afterwards, after that clash, became of the journey of the war-wolves who led away Lot and the people's goods, the treasure of the southern men, and boasted of victory.
Then a man quickly set out, one survivor of the spears, who had come through the battle, to seek Abraham.
He made known that work of war to the Hebrew nobleman: the people of Sodom badly slaughtered, the flower of the people, and Lot's fate.

Then Abraham told that grievous news to his friends; the faithful hero asked his dear companions for help, Aner and Mamre, and Eshcol the third; he said that it was painful to his mind, the sorest of sorrows, that his nephew was suffering servitude;
he asked those battle-bold warriors to devise a plan for this, so that his loyal kinsman might be rescued, the man together with his wife.

Then the three brothers, courageous, at that speech greatly eased his heart's sorrow with firm words, and gave Abraham pledges that they would avenge his injury with him upon the hostile ones, or fall in the slaughter.

Then the holy man ordered his household troop to take up their weapons. He found there warriors, spear-bearers, eighteen and three hundred as well, loyal to their lord, every one of whom he knew could well carry the fallow linden shield in an army.
Then Abraham set out, together with the three nobles who had earlier given him their pledge, with their band of troops; above all he wished to free his kinsman Lot from his enemies' harm.
The men were brave; they carried their shields boldly forward along the road.

The battle-wolves had come near the army camps. Then he, the son of Terah, a wise-minded man, told his chief men in words that there was great need for them to show the strangers, on two sides, a grim meeting in battle, hard hand-play;
He said that the holy, eternal Lord could easily grant him success in that spear-strife.
then, I have heard, the warriors ventured into battle under the shadow of night. There was a din in the camps of shields and shafts, a falling of bowmen, a grinding of war-arrows;
sharp spears cruelly gripped men beneath their garments, and the lives of the foes fell thick, there where, laughing, men and companions had carried off plunder.

Victory, the spear-glory of men, turned back again from the hostile oppression of the Northmen. Abraham gave battle as pledge for his nephew, not twisted gold; he struck and felled the foe in the fight.
The Guardian of the kingdom of heaven took hold to help him. The four armies were put to flight, the kings of the peoples, the leaders of the nations.
Behind him stood a joyful hearth-troop, and the warriors lay, sat [?] on the track, those who had robbed Sodom and Gomorrah of gold and plundered them [?] (stigwitum).
Lot's uncle paid them back harshly for that. The chief troops of the Elamites were in flight, stripped of their glory, until they were not far from Damascus.
Then Abraham went to see the retreat of the hateful men along the battle-road. Lot was rescued, the nobleman with his possessions; the women returned, wives as they wished.

Far and wide they saw birds tearing the slayers of free men amid the sword-slaughter. Abraham brought treasure and brides back to the men of the south, the children of nobles, nearer to their homeland, maidens to their kinsmen.
Never did any man of all the living here carry out a war-expedition more worthily with a small troop, of those who charged against so great a force.

Then southward from there the news of the battle was carried to the people of Sodom: how the departure of the fierce foes had come about. The lord of the people, bereft of his warriors and destitute of friends, went to seek Abraham.

The guardian of treasure travelled to him from Salem. That was the famous Melchizedek, bishop of the people. He came with gifts to greet the leader of warriors, Abraham, graciously and with honour. He set God's blessing upon him and spoke thus:
"May you be honoured among the number of men in the eyes of Him who gave you glory of spears in battle!
That is God himself, who broke the might of the hostile armies into his power, and let you with your weapons clear a broad, bold road forward, rescue the plunder and fell the warriors.

They lay on the track; the expeditionary host could not prosper in battle, but God put them to flight, he who in the fight alongside the chieftains shielded [?] you with his hands against the terror of overwhelming force; and so did the holy covenant which you rightly keep with the Guardian of the heavens."
Then the man gave him a reward for the blessing by his hand, and Abraham gave a tenth part of all that war-booty to God's bishop.
Then the war-king, the lord of Sodom, deprived of his men, spoke to Abraham (he was in need of favour). [?]

"Give me the servants of my people, whom you rescued by the strength of your army from the deadly grip of men! Keep for yourself the twisted gold that once belonged to our people, the wealth and treasures!
Let me lead the children of nobles back, free, to their homeland, to their desolate dwellings: women and boys, poor widows!
The sons are dead, the companions of the people, except for a few alone, who were to guard the borders with me."
Then Abraham answered him at once before the nobles, honoured for his courage, glory and victory; he spoke in lordly manner:
"I promise you, ruler of heroes, by the Holy One who is Lord and owner of the heavens and of this earth, by my words, that there is no worldly wealth that I wish to own, not a penny nor a shilling,

of what of yours I rescued from the bowmen, famous prince, protector of nobles, lest you afterwards say to your dear companions that I became rich on earth through the ancient treasures of the kingdom of Sodom;
but you yourself may lead the plunder away from here, which I won for you in battle, all except the share of these noble warriors, Aner and Mamre and Eshcol.

I will not deprive those men of their right, for they supported me in the clash of spears and fought for your relief. Go now and carry home the adorned gold and the kinswomen, the women of the people."

"For a while you need not fear the battle-rush of hostile warriors, the warfare of the northmen; instead, carrion birds will sit bloody under the mountain-slopes, thickly filled with the slaughter of the nation's armies."
Then the ruler set out on his journey home with the plunder that the holy man had given him, the man of the Hebrews, mindful of honours.

Then once again the high King of the heavens himself spoke holy words to Abraham, encouraged the good-minded man and said to him: "Your rewards are great! Do not let your spirit grow slack, you who are steadfast in my will!
"You need not dread anything as long as you follow my teaching. While you live here I will cover and shield you with my hands against every woe; you need not be afraid."
Then Abraham, bold in deeds and old in his count of days, answered his Lord and asked him: "What will you give me, Ruler of spirits, as a comfort to free men, now that I am so destitute?
I need not build up an inherited seat for any heir of mine; instead, after me my worldly kinsmen will share out my wealth.
You have given me no son, and so sorrow troubles my mind greatly. I myself cannot think of any plan.
"My steward goes about glad with his freeborn children; he firmly intends in his thoughts that his sons shall be my heirs after me."
See: no children have been born to me from my bride."
Then God at once answered him: "Never will stewards control the inheritance of your heirs. Instead, your own child will hold the treasures when your flesh lies dead.
Look at heaven and count its ornaments, the stars of the sky, which now spread their glorious beauty far and wide, shining brightly over the broad waters.
Such will be the multitude of your kindred, strong in offspring. Do not let your spirit be bound by sorrows."
"A son will yet be born to you, a child come from your bride by birth, who will afterward be the guardian of the inheritance, famous before God. Do not mourn!
I am the Ruler who many winters ago led you out of the city of the Chaldeans, as one of four, and promised you wide dwelling-places to rule over.

"Now, kinsman of the Hebrews, I give you my covenant: your land shall be settled with your offspring, many a broad land, the regions of the earth as far as the Euphrates, and from the borders of the Egyptians, as far among men as the Nile divides, and again to the Mediterranean, a wide kingdom.
Your descendants shall own all of that, every one of the nations, as far as the three waters, the foaming floods, wind their streams around the high stone cities, the dwelling-places of the peoples."
Then Sarah was sore at heart that no child had been born to her and Abraham together through their sharing a bed, a noble child to comfort them.

Then, anxious at heart, she began to speak these words to her husband: "The Ruler of the heavens has denied me this: that I might increase the number of your kindred under the skies with children of yours.
Now I have no hope that the support of a family line will ever be granted to the two of us together. I am old and sad!
My lord, do as I ask you!
Here is a maiden, a fair woman, an Egyptian lady, in our power.
"Go quickly to her bed, then, and find out whether the Lord will let any heir of yours come into the world through that woman."
Then the blessed man agreed to the woman's counsel. As his wife advised, he told the serving-woman to go to bed with him.
Her mind grew proud when she had become pregnant with offspring by Abraham.

Out of spite she began to harass her mistress. Bound by the neck [?] as she was, she was arrogant and hostile. She would not willingly endure servitude, but boldly began to struggle hard against Sarah.
Then, as I have heard, the woman made the sorrow of her mind known in words to her lord. Sore at heart she spoke and said forcefully: "You do not act fittingly or rightly toward me.
You have even allowed my handmaid to torment me shamefully every day in deeds and words, ever since Hagar went up to your bed in place of your wife [?], as I had asked."
"Hagar shall pay for that, if you let me rule my own servant, dear Abraham. May the Almighty, Lord of lords, judge this between the two of us."
The wise-minded man answered her at once with his words: "I will not leave you without honour while we both live. You may treat your own serving-woman as your heart pleases."
Then Abraham's queen grew unhappy. Angry in mind at her serving-woman, harsh and fierce, she spoke hostile and cruel words to the woman.
Then the woman fled from oppression and servitude. She would not endure harm and punishment for what she had earlier done to Sarah, so she set out on a journey to seek the wilderness.
There a thane of glory, an angel of the Lord, met her alone and sad at heart, and he asked her earnestly: "Where are you hurrying, destitute woman, on these journeys? Sarah owns you."
She at once answered him: "Lacking every joy, I fled in misery from the dwellings, from woe, my lady's hatred, grief and injury."
"Now I must wait in the wilderness with tears on my cheeks for my fate, until hunger or the wolf tears soul and sorrow together from my heart."

Then the angel answered her: "Do not try to break off the companionship between the two of you by fleeing far from here. Instead, go back and earn favour for yourself. Humbly begin to serve as your duties require, and be loyal to your lord."
"Hagar, you shall bring a son into the world for Abraham. With these words of mine I tell you now that the boy shall be called Ishmael among men.
He will be fierce and eager for battle, an enemy to the families of men, to his own kin. Many will fight against him in anger with violent weapons.
From that founder peoples will spring, a countless nation. Go back now to your master; stay with those who own you!"
Then she at once went back to her lord and lady, following the angel's teaching, as the holy one, God's messenger-spirit, had commanded her in wise speech.
Then Ishmael was born to Abraham, just when he had lived eighty-six winters in the world.
The son grew and thrived, as the angel, the faithful messenger of peace, had told the woman in his own words.
Then after thirteen years the Prince, the eternal Lord, spoke with Abraham: "Beloved, keep our covenant well, as I instruct you!

I will raise you up in prosperity at all times. Be firm in doing my will! From now on I will faithfully keep the covenant that I gave you long ago as a pledge of comfort, for which your spirit had mourned.
"You shall sanctify your household.
Set the true sign of victory on every male, if you want to have in me a lord or a loyal friend to your offspring.
I will be the shepherd and guardian of that people, if you obey me in the thoughts of your hearts and are willing to fulfil my commands.

Every male of that lineage who comes into the world shall be dedicated to me as a child after seven nights with the sign of victory, or else be cut off far from the earth in enmity and driven from all good things. Do as I command!"
I will keep faith with you, if you take on that sign of true faith. You shall have a son, a child by your wife, whom all the city-dwellers shall call Isaac.
You need not be ashamed of that heir. Rather, I will give that young man my divine grace through the powers of the spirit, an abundance of friends, along with benefits.

He shall receive my bliss and blessing, love and favour. From that founder of the people a broad nation shall come. Many lords shall rise up valiant, guardians of the kingdom, kings of the world, widely famous."
Abraham then quickly laid his face on the ground, and in his heart and mind he turned the spoken words over with scorn.

Abraham himself did not expect from that day's speech that Sarah, his grey-haired wife, could bring a son into the world. He knew well that the woman had indeed reached a full hundred winters, counted by number.

Then, old in years, he answered the Creator: "Likewise may Ishmael live by your teachings, Lord, and bear you thanks, a resolute mind and a strong heart, to carry out your will day and night in words and deeds."
Then the almighty Lord, the eternal Lord, answered him graciously: "Sarah, old in winters, shall bring a son into the world for you. Truly, events shall go forward according to these spoken terms.

I will gladly bless Ishmael now, as you are asking for your firstborn, so that he may live to see many days of life in the kingdom of the world, with branches of offspring. Let that be granted to you!

Yet I will raise up more greatly Isaac, your heir, the young child who has not yet come into the world, with abundant goods and every excellence in his days. I will truly keep with him my covenant of the mind, holy and faithful intentions, and I will be gracious to him."
Abraham did as the Eternal had commanded him. At the Lord's bidding he set the sign of peace upon his own son, and ordered every high-ranking man to bear that sign,
[?] who was of his household, of the male kind. Mindful of the covenant and wise in mind, when God gave him true pledges, he then received the bright sign himself.

The Creator, the glorious King, ever increased his fame with excellences in the kingdom of the world. Abraham had earned this from him, since from the very first on his journey he was able to carry out his Ruler's will.

Then the woman laughed at the Lord of hosts, not at all gladly. Old in years, she mocked that spoken promise bitterly in her mind. She did not believe the truth, that fulfilment would follow that speech.
When the Ruler of the heavens heard that Abraham's wife had broken into hopeless laughter in her chamber, holy God said:
"Sarah will not believe the truth of my words. Yet what is fated shall go forward just as I promised you at the beginning.
I tell you truly: at this same time an heir will be born of the woman.
When I visit this same dwelling a second time, my promises to you will be fulfilled. You will look on a son, your own child, dear Abraham!"

After that speech the holy spirits, eager to go elsewhere, quickly set out from the place of speaking and travelled with speed. They left their tracks behind them, and Lot's kinsman himself went with them as a companion, until they could look upon Sodom, the steep-walled city.
They saw halls towering over treasure, buildings over red gold. Then the Ruler of the skies, gracious to Abraham, began to speak and told him no small news:

"In this city I hear an uproar, the very loud cry of sinners, the boasting of the ale-merry. The crowd within the walls uses evil speech. Therefore the sins of the people, the oath-breakers, are heavy.
"Kinsman of the Hebrews, I will now find out what those men are doing, whether they commit sins as greatly in their habits and thoughts as they perversely speak deceit and malice;
"Fire shall avenge that: brimstone and black flame, painful and grim, hot and violent, upon the heathen people."
The men, and their wives with them, awaited punishment and woe within their walls.

Proud in their prosperity, they repaid the Lord's goodness with wickedness, until the Protector of spirits, the source of the light of life, would no longer endure the offence. The stern-minded King sent two strong messengers of his to them, and at eventide they made their way to the city of Sodom.
Then at the city gate they met the man himself, the son of Haran, sitting there, and to that wise man they looked like young men.

Then the servant of the Lord rose up to meet the visitors and went to greet the strangers courteously. He kept in mind the right and fitting custom of his people, and he offered the men lodging for the night.
Then the noble messengers of the Saviour answered him: "Thank you for the kindness you have offered the two of us!
We two mean to stay quietly by this street and wait for the right time, until the Lord lets the sun rise again tomorrow morning."

Then Lot bowed down at the feet of the guests and urged them to accept rest, meals, the shelter of his house, and his service. They gratefully accepted the nobleman's kindness and went at once, as the Hebrew nobleman directed them, in under his roof.
There the noble, wise-minded man gave them fine hospitality in his hall, until the evening light had gone.
Then night came, following on the heels of day. With darkness it covered the ocean streams, the splendour of this life, the seas and the broad lands.
Then the people of Sodom came, young and old, hateful to God, in great crowds, demanding the strangers, so that they surrounded Lot and his guests with the strength of an army.

They demanded that the holy messengers be led out of the high house, that the men be handed over to them. They said openly that they wanted to lie with the men shamelessly, and they cared nothing for decency.
Then Lot, who had often shown wise judgement, rose quickly in the house and went straight out. Then the son of Haran, mindful of wisdom, spoke before the whole band of nobles:
"Here inside are my two daughters, undefiled. Do as I ask you (neither of these women has yet known a man's closeness through sharing his bed), and give up this sin.
I will give them to you before you commit a shameful act against nature, a boundless evil among the children of men.
Take the young women and leave my guests in peace. For God's sake I want to protect them from you, if I can."
Then the crowd, that wicked race, answered him with one voice: "It seems fitting and entirely right that you should take yourself away from this nation.
You came to this people from far away, on an exile's path, poor in friends, with no one to protect you.
Do you want, if you can manage it, to be our chief judge here and the people's teacher?" Then, I have heard, the heathen fighting men seized Lot with their hands, with hostile hands.

His guests helped him well. The merciful strangers pulled him out of the grip of those fierce men and back in under the roof. Then they quickly and firmly sealed the eyes of every one of the people of Sodom standing around.
At once the whole crowd of townspeople went blind. Fierce as they were, they could not break into the house to get the guests, as they had tried to, because God's messengers were strong there.
The guests had great strength, and they rebuked the crowd harshly with punishment. Then the faithful messengers of peace spoke kindly to Lot:
"If you have a son or a dear relative, or any friend among these people besides these women we see here,
lead those who are dear to you out of this city, in great haste, and save your life, so that you do not die with these faithless men.

The Ruler has commanded the two of us, because of the people's sins, to give Sodom and Gomorrah to the black flame, to fire. We are to kill these people, the inhabitants of the cities, with deadly violence, and carry out his anger.
That time is very near. Go and save your life on the road. The Lord is merciful to you."
Lot answered him at once: "With the women I cannot travel so far from here on foot to find safety for my life. You two kindly show me love and friendship, and you grant me loyalty and favour.
"I know a high city near here, a little town. Grant me mercy and rest there, so that we may go up to Zoar to seek refuge for our lives."
If you two are willing to protect that stronghold firmly from the fire, we can safely wait in that place for better fortune and save our lives." Then the gracious angels answered him kindly:
"Your request about the city shall be granted. Hurry quickly to the stronghold. We two will keep you in peace and under our protection.
We may not avenge God's anger on the oath-breakers, or put the sinful race to death, until you have led your children and your wife together into Zoar."

Then Abraham's kinsman hurried to the stronghold. The man did not spare his feet as he went with the women, but he made his way forward in haste until he had led his wife and children under the town's walls, into Zoar.

Just as the sun, the peace-candle of the peoples, had risen, I have heard that the Lord of heaven sent sulphur from the heavens and black flame, boiling fire, as punishment on those men, because in former days they had long provoked the Lord.
The Ruler of spirits paid them back for it! A great affliction seized the heathen race. A din arose in the cities, the cry of the wicked at the onset of death, of the hateful race.
The flame consumed everything green it found within the golden cities, and burning and terror were also sent far and wide over no small part of the broad earth round about.
The groves became ash and embers, the fruits of the earth, just as far as the fierce punishments reached across the wide land of men.

The plundering fire, the roaring flame, swallowed up together everything, high and broad, that men owned in the city of Sodom and in Gomorrah. God, the Lord, destroyed all of it together with the people.

When Lot's wife heard in the towns that crash of fire, the people being parted from life, she looked back behind her toward that slaughter. The writings tell us that she at once became the likeness of a pillar of salt.
Ever after, the image (that is a famous story) remained standing still where a strong punishment had seized her, because she would not obey the words of the thegns of glory.
Now, hard and steep, she must await her fate in that place, the Lord's judgment, when the count of days, the world, shall pass away. That is one of the wonders that the Lord of glory has worked.

Then Abraham went off alone at early dawn, so that he stood again where he, the wise patriarch, had earlier spoken in words with his Ruler. He saw a deadly smoke rising from the earth and flying far and wide.

Pride and wine-drinking had come upon them, so that they became too bold in wicked deeds, daring in sins; they forgot truth, the Lord's judgments, and who had given them prosperity and glory in their cities. Therefore the Prince of angels sent them surging-hot flame as punishment.
Then our faithful Ruler graciously remembered Abraham, as he often did his beloved man. He saved Lot, that man's kinsman, when the multitude perished.

The brave man did not dare, for fear of the Lord, to live any longer in that stronghold. Instead Lot went out of the town, and his children with him, to look for a dwelling farther from the place of slaughter, until they found a cave in the slope of a high mountain.
There the blessed Lot, faithful to his covenant and dear to the Ruler, lived for a great number of days, and his two daughters with him.
They did so; the elder went first to the bed of their father, the father of both of them, when he was drunk.

The grey-haired man did not know when the two young women were each with him as a bride, for in the chamber of his heart his mind and memory were firmly fettered, so that, drunk with wine, he could not know what the women were doing.
The women became pregnant; the willing sisters brought children into the world, sons of their old father.
The mother of one of those princes, Lot's daughter, who was the elder in years, named him Moab. The writings, the divine books, tell us that the younger called her own child Ammon.
From those founders arose a countless multitude, two mighty nations.
All the dwellers on earth call one of those tribes, a widely known race, the Moabites; men name the other, the children of princes, the Ammonites.
Then Haran's brother went with his wife and his household to bring his possessions into the land of Abimelech.
Abraham told the men in his words that Sarah was his sister (he was protecting his life), because he knew well that he had few friends or kinsmen among that people.
Then the prince sent his thanes and ordered them to bring her to him.
Then for a second time Abraham's wife, a foreigner, was taken from her husband into a stranger's embrace.
Then the eternal Lord, our Saviour, helped him there, as he often did. He came himself by night to where the ruler lay drunk with wine.
Then the true King began to speak through a dream to the prince and angrily threatened him: "You have taken Abraham's woman, the bride from her husband.
"... for that deed death shall tear your soul out of your breast." The giver of treasure, weary from feasting, answered him in his sleep:
"Lo, Lord of angels, will you ever in your anger take the life of, and cut down [?], one who lives here by right customs, is firm in counsel and in mind, and seeks mercy from you?
"That woman herself told me earlier in her own words, without my asking, that she was Abraham's sister. I have not sinned with her, and have not yet committed any wrong."

Then at once the eternal Lord, the true Creator, spoke to him again through that dream: "Give back to Abraham his lady, his wife, into his keeping, if you, protector of nobles, care any longer for life in the world.
He is good and wise; he can himself speak with God and see the King of heaven. You shall die, together with your wealth and your household, if you withhold his bride from the patriarch.

He can intercede for you, if he, courteous and patient, will quickly deliver your message to me, so that I may still let you, while you live, enjoy favours and benefits in your days, safe in your treasure."
Then the guardian of the people started up from sleep in fear. He ordered his counsellors to be fetched to him, and Abimelech, oppressed by terror, told the nobles in full the words of the Ruler.
Because of that deed and after that dream, the men feared a blow from the Lord's hand. Then the king himself ordered Abraham to come to him in great haste.

Then the mighty prince spoke: "Hebrew kinsman, tell me in words: how did I bring it about, after you, Abraham, led your possessions among us into this homeland, that you plotted such a great deceit against me?

You, a foreigner, wished to ensnare us with deceit in this nation and to defile us with sins. You said in words that Sarah was your sister, your kinswoman by blood. Hatefully, you wished to bring guilt upon me through that woman, an immense evil.
We entertained you honourably, and in friendship we assigned you a dwelling among this people, and land as a favour. Now you repay us, and thank us unkindly for our kindnesses!"
Then Abraham answered: "I did not do it out of deceit or enmity, or for any reason that would mean I wished you harm.
But, lord of men, far from my kinsmen, I protected myself by cunning against the blow of the war-shield, ever since the Holy One, the Lord, long ago led me out of my father's household.
Since then I have sought out many peoples and unknown friends, and this woman has been with me, without friends.
I was always living in expectation of that danger: that some hostile man would take my life, since I was a foreigner, because he wanted to have this lady for himself afterwards.
Therefore I told the warriors in words that Sarah was my sister, everywhere on earth where the two of us, without a homeland, had to struggle among foreigners.
I endured the same fear in this homeland, after I chose your protection, famous prince.
When I first came here, I did not know in my mind whether there was fear of the Almighty Lord among this people.
Therefore I hid the true account from your thegns, and most of all from you yourself: that Sarah had come to my bed as my bride."
Then Abimelech began to enrich Abraham with worldly treasures and gave him back his wife.
Because he had taken his wife, he gave him livestock, bright silver and female servants as compensation. Then the protector of princes also spoke these words to Abraham:
"Live with us, and choose a dwelling-place for yourself as your homeland, wherever in this land is dearest to you, in this land that I shall possess.
Be a faithful friend to us, and we will give you wealth!"
Then the giver of treasure quickly spoke again to Sarah with other words:

"Abraham, your lord and master, need not hold it against you as a reproach that you, woman bright as an elf, walked the floors of my hall; instead, I will make full amends to him in white silver for the injury to his feelings.
You two need not seek benefits elsewhere, away from this homeland, among unknown friends; instead, live here."
Abraham did as his Lord commanded him and, at the Lord's bidding, accepted friendship with love and favours. He was dear to God.
Therefore he lived blessed in peace and went under the shadow of his Creator, covered by sheltering wings, while he lived here.

But God was still angry with Abimelech for the sin he had committed earlier against Sarah and Abraham, when he separated the two dear ones, the woman and the man. For that he received suffering, a severe punishment.

Neither free women nor slave women could increase the number of people for their lords by bearing children, because the Creator prevented it, until the holy Abraham began to ask the eternal Lord for mercy for his lord.

The protector of angels granted his request. He unlocked fertility for the people's king, for free and slave, for men and women. The Ruler of the heavens let their number grow again, along with their riches and possessions.
The Almighty, guardian of mankind, became gentle in mind toward Abimelech, as Abraham had asked him.
Then the Lord almighty, our Ruler, came to Sarah, just as he himself had said. The Prince of life had kept his spoken promise to the man and the woman he loved.
A child was born to Abraham from his bride. The Prince of angels had named him Isaac before the mother was pregnant with that offspring by her husband.
With his own hand Abraham set the sign upon him, as the Lord, glorious and bright, had commanded him, one week after his mother brought him into the world among mankind.
The boy grew and thrived, as was natural for him, being noble from his forebears. Abraham was a hundred years old when his wife bore him a son, to his joy.
He had waited a long time for this, ever since the Lord first announced the joyful day to him through his own word.
Then it came about that the woman saw Ishmael playing in front of Abraham, where the two of them sat at the feast, holy in mind, and all their household drank and made merry.

Then the noble woman, the wife, said to her husband: "Grant me this, guardian of rings, my dear lord: order Hagar to go elsewhere and to take Ishmael with her! We will no longer live together if I have my way, if I may decide it."
Ishmael shall never share the inheritance with Isaac, with my own child, after you are gone, when you send the life out of your body."
Then Abraham was grieved in his mind that he should drive his own son into exile. Then the true Lord graciously came to help him; he knew that the man's spirit was in the fetters of cares.
The King of angels, the eternal Lord, spoke to Abraham: "Let the sorrow slip from your breast, the strife of your mind, and listen to the woman, your wife!
Order both of them to go away, Hagar and Ishmael, the boy, out of the homeland! I will make his kin broad and mighty in offspring of children, rich in fruit, as I promised you in words."
Then the man obeyed his Ruler. Sad at heart, he drove the two from the dwellings: the woman from the land, and his own child.
"It is clear and plain that the true Lord, Prince of the heavens, is with you as a companion, he who grants victory, with wisdom, by his powers, and strengthens your mind with divine gifts.
Therefore you have always prospered in whatever you have undertaken, toward friend or foe, in words or in deeds. The Ruler, the Lord, pushes your will forward on its way with his hands.

That is widely known to the city-dwellers. Now I ask you with my words, friend of the Hebrews, that you, with good will, give pledges, your covenants, that you will be a faithful friend to me in reward for the benefits
that I have done you for your good, ever since you came destitute from far away into this nation, on an exile's track.
Repay me with favour, since I was not stingy toward you with land and kindnesses.

Be gracious now to this people and to my kindred, if the All-Ruler, our Lord, who governs what is ordained, wills to grant you that you may more widely in this nation share out treasures to shield-warriors, the wealth of proud men, and set boundaries."
Then Abraham gave Abimelech a pledge that he would do so.

Afterwards the blessed son of Terah, the man of the Hebrews, was settled for a long time among the people of the Philistines, poor among strangers. The Lord of angels showed him a dwelling place, which the city-dwellers call the land of Beersheba.

There the holy man built a lofty, high hall, a city, and planted a grove, and made an altar. In that bright place he offered sacrifice to his Ruler, abundant offerings, to him who gave him life, blessed under the heavens.
Then the mighty King began to test the man and eagerly tried what the courage of the noble one was like. In stern words he spoke to him aloud:
"Go quickly, Abraham, set out on the road, and take your own child with you. You must sacrifice Isaac, your son, to me, yourself, as an offering.
When you have climbed a steep hill, the ridge of the high land that I will show you from here, going up on your own feet, there you shall prepare a pyre,
[?] … a funeral fire for your child, and sacrifice your son yourself with the edge of the sword, and then burn the body of the beloved one with black flame and offer me the sacrifice."
He did not delay the journey but at once began to hurry to set out. The word of the Lord of angels was awe-inspiring to him, and his Ruler was dear to him.

Then the blessed Abraham left his night's rest. He did not scorn the Saviour's command at all. The holy man girded himself with a grey sword, and showed that fear of the Guardian of spirits dwelt in his breast.
Then the old-hearted giver of gold began to bridle his asses, and he ordered two young men to travel with him.
His own kinsman was the third, and he himself the fourth. Then he set out eagerly from his own dwelling, leading Isaac, the ungrown child, as the Creator had commanded him.
Then he hurried greatly and pressed forward along the road, as the Lord had shown him the ways across the wilderness, until the glory-bright dawn of the third day rose up over the deep water.
Then the blessed man saw a high mountain towering, as the Lord of heaven had told him before.
Then Abraham spoke to his servants: "My men, rest here, the two of you, at this camp. The two of us will come back once we have carried out our errand to the King of spirits."
Then the prince and his own son went to the place that the Lord had shown him, making their way through the forests. The son carried the wood, the father the fire and the sword.
Then the man young in years began to ask Abraham about this: "My lord, we two have fire and a sword here. Where is the offering that you mean to bring to God, the bright one, as a burnt offering?"
Abraham spoke (he had firmly resolved to do as the Lord had commanded him): "The true King, the Guardian of mankind, will find that for himself, as seems fitting to him."

Then the resolute man climbed up the steep mountain with his son, as the Eternal One had commanded him, so that he stood on the summit of the high land, in the place that the strong and faithful Lord had shown him in words.

Then he began to build the pyre and kindle the fire. He fettered the feet and hands of his child, lifted young Isaac onto the pyre, and quickly grasped the sword by the hilt. He meant to kill his son with his own hands and give the fire his kinsman's blood to drink.
Then the Lord's servant, one of the angels from above, called to Abraham in a loud voice. He waited quietly for the messenger's words and answered the angel.

Then God's glorious spirit quickly spoke to him in words from the heavens above: "Dear Abraham, do not kill your own child, but take the boy, your son, alive from the pyre! The God of glory favours him!
Man of the Hebrews, you yourself shall receive rewards by the hand of the holy one, the King of heaven: true rewards of victory and ample gifts.
The Guardian of spirits will repay you graciously, because his friendship and favour were dearer to you than your own child."
The pyre stood kindled. The Creator of mankind had gladdened the heart of Abraham, kinsman of Lot, when he gave him back his child, Isaac, alive.
Then the blessed man, the warrior, looked over his shoulder and saw a ram standing there alone, not far away, the brother of Aaron [?], caught fast in brambles.
Abraham took it and lifted it onto the pyre with great haste in place of his own son.

Then he drew the blade and sprinkled the burnt offering, the smoking [?] altar, with the ram's blood. He sacrificed that offering to God and gave thanks for the rewards and for all the blessings that the Lord of gifts had granted him, later and earlier.
